To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the fine structure of chromatin in isolated nuclei is dependent on the presence of histone proteins, (ii) the fine structure is dependent on the pH of fixation and (iii) the gross distribution of chromatin in nuclei is not dependent on histone proteins.

the histone proteins are responsible for the fine structure of chromatin, and that the gross structure of the chromatin is determined by a combination of the histone proteins and the non-histone chromosomal proteins.
the fine structure of nuclei is altered in a predictable manner by the sequential extraction of histones.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the structural organization of nuclear chromatin.
the structure of chromatin and its relationship to the organization of genetic material.
the structure of the cell nucleus and the organization of chromatin within this subcellular organelle.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the histones, and possibly non-histone nuclear proteins, play a significant role in determining the fine structure of chromatin, but the gross organization is probably due to the combined effect of the nuclear membrane and the nuclear proteins.

histones I, II and V, which are the most soluble histones, are responsible for maintaining the 200 A diameter fibrils of the chromatin in the nucleus and that the other histone fractions, which are more tightly bound to the chromatin, contribute to the gross organization of the chromatin.
histones are not responsible for the gross organization of the chromatin in situ but that they are responsible for the fine structure of the chromatin fibrils.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
histones are responsible for the tertiary structure of chromatin, while the secondary organization is a function of the histone proteins plus the nuclear membrane.
histone proteins are important in the fine organization and distribution of chromatin fibrils within the nucleus but are not the sole determinant of the gross organization of heterochromatine masses.
the structural organization of nuclei is not a simple reflection of the histones and that histones do not act alone in maintaining the integrity of nuclear structures.
The main takeaway from our work is that
histones are not only responsible for the primary structure of chromatin, but also for the secondary and tertiary structure.
there are many different histone proteins, and that they have very different effects on the structure of the chromatin.
the structural organization of the nucleus is a dynamic process and that histone proteins play a key role in this process.
